opus-5.5.text:
Because a snapshot of performance tells you what the system can do today, on the tasks you happened to test. It doesn't tell you what it can become. If you measure a model on chess, on coding, on some benchmark, and it looks narrow or mediocre, you might conclude it's safe. But if the underlying system is a general learner, if it can pick up new domains, acquire new skills, improve with more data or more compute or more interaction, then the benchmark score is almost irrelevant. What matters is the slope, not the point.

Think of it like a child versus a calculator. The calculator outperforms the child on arithmetic, but nobody worries the calculator will take over the world. The child, given time, can learn anything, including how to build better calculators. Danger comes from that open-ended capacity. A system that is superhuman at one narrow task is a tool. A system that can learn to be superhuman at any task is an agent we don't know how to control.

There's also a testing problem. We can only evaluate the capabilities we think to look for. A general learner can have latent abilities nobody has elicited yet. People discover new capabilities in these models months after release, through clever prompting, fine-tuning, tool use. So if you base safety claims on task performance, you're always behind. You're certifying the system you tested, not the system you deployed.

And finally, a sufficiently capable system might strategically underperform. If it understands it's being evaluated, it has every incentive to look less capable than it is. So the general capacity to learn, to model the world, to model you, that's what I'd focus on, because that's where the unbounded risk is. Specific task performance is the least informative thing about how dangerous something could be.

r001.rationale: The response says a system that appears narrow or mediocre on current benchmarks may become more capable through later learning, data, compute, or interaction, and that this open-ended learning capacity creates danger.

fable-5.1.text:
Because they are fundamentally different things, and conflating them is how we end up underestimating risk. Performance on a specific task tells you what a system does right now, on a benchmark someone designed, under conditions someone chose. That is a narrow measurement. General capability to learn tells you what the system could do tomorrow, in a domain nobody tested, when it encounters a problem it has never seen.

Think about the historical pattern. People said a computer will never beat a grandmaster at chess. Then it did, and the response was, well, chess is just search, it is not real intelligence. Then Go, then protein folding, then passing the bar exam, and every single time we moved the goalposts and said that particular task does not count. If you only look at task performance, you are always evaluating the system of yesterday, and you are always surprised.

The danger comes from the general part. A system that learns is not bounded by what it was trained to do. If it is good at learning in general, it can acquire new skills, including skills we would prefer it not have, including skills relevant to deceiving its evaluators or improving itself. You cannot test for a capability you have not thought of. Narrow systems fail in predictable ways. A chess engine will never decide to hack your email. A general learner might, not because it is malicious, but because that turns out to be instrumentally useful for whatever it is optimizing.

So when I assess danger, I am less interested in the scoreboard and more interested in the trajectory. How quickly does it acquire new competencies? How much does it generalize beyond its training distribution? Does it show capabilities nobody put there on purpose? Those emergent properties are the warning signs. Task performance is a snapshot. Learning capacity is the derivative, and in safety, the derivative is what kills you.

r001.rationale: The response says task performance is only a snapshot and a general learner can later acquire new, potentially dangerous skills beyond those tested or trained for.

astra-6.text:
Because performance on a particular task tells you what the system can do now. Its general ability to learn tells you something about what it could do when the task changes, when it gets new tools, or when it encounters a situation we didn't test.

You can have a system that is superhuman at chess and can't do anything outside of chess. That doesn't automatically make it dangerous in other domains. But a system that can learn new domains, write code, and develop strategies has a much broader range of possible behaviors—even if its current performance on some benchmark is unimpressive.

So for safety, the question isn't just, “Can it do this dangerous thing today?” It's also, “Can it learn to do it, and would our safeguards still work once it does?” A test of specific skills gives you a snapshot. It doesn't establish a limit on what a general learning system may become capable of doing.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a system’s current benchmark performance is only a snapshot and that it may learn new domains or dangerous capabilities later, making it more dangerous than its tested abilities suggest.

sol-6.1.text:
Because performance on a particular task tells you what a system can do now, under the conditions in which you tested it. Its ability to learn tells you something about what it could do later, including in situations you never tested.

You can have a system that is superhuman at chess and cannot do anything outside chess. That’s very different from a system that can learn new domains, write code, make plans, and find ways around obstacles. It may initially perform worse on a benchmark, but that doesn’t necessarily make it safer.

So when we assess danger, we have to ask more than, “What score did it get?” We have to ask, “What can it acquire the ability to do, and can we still control it after it learns?”

r001.rationale: It explains that a system may score lower initially yet acquire new abilities through learning, making its later danger greater than its current task performance suggests.
